newsitem.title: USA: EU, U.S. officials brace for late night meat talks.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. officials brace for late night meat talks.

text.p: EU and U.S. officials were gearing up for a late night Tuesday as they resumed talks to resolve a nasty dispute that threatens to disrupt the trade of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of meat and poultry.

The senior European Union negotiator at the bilateral talks on meat import inspection regulations predicted "tough discussions" ahead in the next few days as negotiators make a last-ditch effort to ward off a trade war.

"We've got a couple of days ahead of us with some tough discussions and we'll hope that by the end we'll have some kind of an agreement," EU's Lars Hoelgaard told reporters on his way into talks with U.S. Agriculture Department officials, including senior Agriculture Department trade official Paul Drazek.
EU officials arrived in Washington late Monday night to resume the so-called veterinary equivalency talks that ended last week without agreement by an April 1 deadline.
Negotiators lunched together Tuesday, and officially began talks in mid-afternoon. Discussions were expected to last well into the evening.

Both sides have imposed new meat and poultry inspection regulations that could stop up to $100 million worth of U.S. poultry and dairy products going to Europe and halt some $300 million worth of European meat products, mostly Danish pork products and Italian hams, from being shipped to the United States.
Hoelgaard said the main sticking points were U.S. poultry processing procedures and the use of decontamination.
He said he was scheduled to go back to Brussels Thursday evening "and by then we should know where we are." Hoelgaard said the EU side was hoping to narrow down the remaining differences.

Drazek said late last week that the "complexion of the negotiations" had changed since last week's moves to stop meat and poultry shipments. He said that trade has already been disrupted, and unless an agreement is reached soon, things could only get worse.

Without an agreement, new European restrictions on U.S. poultry will continue, and as of April 15, European meat and poultry plants will not be able to export their products to the United States if they cannot comply with U.S. standards.
U.S. poultry producers said Tuesday they were unwilling to back away from improvements in food safety standards in order to meet the demands of the EU.

The Europeans want the United States to adopt the EU's rules that are "lacking in commitment to overall microbiological quality and wholesomeness," said Kenneth May, technical advisor to the National Broiler Council.

"The European Union officials want us to go back to where we stood 20 years ago and ignore all the scientific findings and technological advancements that have been made in that time," May said in a statement.
